course.title: Atomic Checkpoint Secondary Cambridge Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Energy
unit.blurb: Energy stores and transfers, conservation and dissipation of energy, efficiency, sound waves and echoes, and renewable energy.

O1.t: Name and give examples of energy stores, and use joules and kilojoules.

O2.t: Describe energy transfers (mechanical, electrical, heating, waves) and show them in flow diagrams; energy is conserved.

O3.t: Explain that energy dissipates to the surroundings and compare the efficiency of devices.

O4.t: Explain how sound travels, why it cannot pass through a vacuum, how echoes are used, and why we need renewable energy.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 11: Energy.

At a hydroelectric dam, rushing water spins turbines that turn a generator, making electricity. You use energy every time you throw a ball, switch on a light or boil water. But what is energy, and how does it get from one place to another?
Energy can be stored and used later. Moving objects have kinetic energy. The faster an object moves, the more kinetic energy it has, so a speeding truck has lots of it.
Objects above the ground store gravitational potential energy. If two identical books sit at different heights, the higher one stores more.
Chemical energy is stored in the bonds that hold atoms together. Food, fuels and batteries are chemical energy stores. When it's released, it can power things, including you!

Energy is measured in joules, named after the scientist James Prescott Joule. One kilojoule is 1000 joules. A large apple stores about 327 kilojoules, a bowl of rice about 536, and a small chocolate bar about 1000 kilojoules!
Objects that are stretched or squashed store elastic potential energy. As you land on a trampoline, its springs stretch and store energy, which then bounces you back up.
Nuclear energy is stored in the nucleus, the centre of an atom. Nuclear power stations use it to generate electricity, though people disagree about whether this is a good option.
Thermal energy is the energy of the particles in an object, mostly their vibrations. Hot geysers, your body, and even ice cubes all have thermal energy!

sections.title: Transferring energy

stops.note: Paused after: “Thermal energy is transferred by heat, from a hotter place to a colder one. On a stove, en”
Paused after: “Some energy from the fuel is also released to the surroundings as heat, light and sound. A”

q.prompt: In a rocket launch, energy starts in the…

captions: Here's a key idea: energy can't be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another. There are four main ways.

Energy can be transferred mechanically, when a force moves an object. When you lift a box, energy is transferred from the chemical store in your muscles to the gravitational potential store of the box.

Energy can be transferred electrically, by a flow of charge. Power stations burn fuels to generate electricity, which flows to our homes. Switch on a fan, and the energy ends up in the kinetic store of the spinning blades. Lightning is a giant electrical transfer from storm clouds!
Thermal energy is transferred by heat, from a hotter place to a colder one. On a stove, energy moves from the flame to the pot, and then to the water inside to cook food.
Energy is also transferred by waves, such as light and sound. Energy from the Sun reaches Earth as light, and plants transfer it into chemical energy when they make food by photosynthesis.

Energy is often transferred in stages. In a rocket launch, burning fuel transfers energy from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store of the rocket. As it climbs, energy goes into its gravitational potential store.
Some energy from the fuel is also released to the surroundings as heat, light and sound. A flow diagram shows all these stores and transfers clearly.

stops.note: Paused after: “A fluorescent lamp gives 80 percent light, and an LED gives 90 percent. The LED is the mos”

q.prompt: What percentage of a tungsten bulb's energy becomes heat?

captions: Hold your hand near a lamp, and you'll feel it's warm. The lamp transfers energy as light, which is useful, and as heat, which is wasted.
Different lamps waste different amounts. An old tungsten bulb turns only 15 percent of its energy into light, and 85 percent into heat.
A fluorescent lamp gives 80 percent light, and an LED gives 90 percent. The LED is the most efficient: it wastes the least electricity.

Most energy transfers waste some energy to the surroundings, usually as heat or sound. The energy spreads out, or dissipates, and becomes less useful. Efficiency tells us how much of the energy we put in is transferred usefully.

sections.title: Sound

stops.note: Paused after: “Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. It's fastest in solids, where the part”
Paused after: “Ships use sonar to map the seabed and find fish or submarines. Doctors use ultrasound, sou”
Paused after: “Hydropower uses the gravitational potential energy of water stored behind a dam. Tidal pow”

captions: Sound is made when objects vibrate. A violin's strings vibrate, making the air particles beside them vibrate too. They bump into their neighbours, passing the energy along as a sound wave, all the way to your ear.

Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. It's fastest in solids, where the particles are closest together. But sound can't travel through a vacuum, because there are no particles to pass the vibrations along. Space is silent!
The more energy a sound wave transfers, the louder the sound. Humans can hear sounds up to about 20 kilohertz, but bats can hear up to 90 kilohertz!
Shout across a canyon, and you hear your voice come back. When sound waves hit a hard surface, some bounce back, or reflect. The reflected sound is an echo.
Echoes are useful! By timing how long an echo takes to return, we can work out how far away an object is. This is echolocation. Bats, dolphins and whales use it to find their prey.
Ships use sonar to map the seabed and find fish or submarines. Doctors use ultrasound, sound too high for us to hear, to build pictures of the inside of the body.

But echoes aren't always wanted. Concert halls and radio studios line their walls with soft materials that absorb sound instead of reflecting it. Some moths even have wing scales that absorb a bat's calls!

Burning fossil fuels harms our planet, so we need more renewable energy resources that never run out. Solar panels transfer the energy of sunlight into electricity, and wind turbines use the kinetic energy of the wind.
Hydropower uses the gravitational potential energy of water stored behind a dam. Tidal power, geothermal power and biofuels are renewable too.
About 30 percent of the world's electricity now comes from renewable sources, and the world's governments have agreed to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030.

Answer: Elastic potential energy.
Question 2: Describe the energy transfer when you lift a box onto a shelf. Pause the video now.

Question 3: A tungsten lamp uses 100 J. How much energy is wasted as heat? Pause the video now.
Answer: 85 J.
Question 4: Why can't sound travel through space? Pause the video now.
Answer: Space is a vacuum – there are no particles to vibrate.
